mappings.note: The section point is parametrised k:1 and substituted into a LINE equation to find k, then the point itself. Ratio of division, so LO-2.

Area of a RHOMBUS via half the product of its diagonals, the diagonals being distances (LO-1). C-4.2-LO-1 names a triangle only, so the area half sits at competency level - a genuine gap in the frame for areas of quadrilaterals from coordinates.
Ratio unknown with fully symbolic coordinates; the k:1 algebra collapses to k = 1. Section formula, not the midpoint outcome, because the 1:1 result is derived rather than assumed.
Equidistant point on the x-axis from two off-axis points, found by squaring distances. Distance outcome.
Similarity argued from the RATIOS OF SIDE LENGTHS, every one of which is a distance computation. No area or section idea is used.

Locates the remaining vertices of an equilateral triangle by equating side lengths. Distance outcome. Stem depends on a figure that does not travel with it - the position of A is only readable from the diagram.
Equidistance squared and expanded to prove 3x = 2y. Distance formula used algebraically.
Ratio unknown, recovered as k:1 from the abscissa, then the ordinate follows. LO-2.
P, Q, R, S are the MIDPOINTS of the rectangle's sides and PQRS is then shown to have diagonals with a common midpoint. Midpoint formula used twice over, exactly LO-3's quadrilateral clause.
Sports-day flags: part (i) is the DISTANCE between the two flags (LO-1) and part (ii) is the halfway point, i.e. the MIDPOINT (LO-3). Two parts, two outcomes.
Compares two journey DISTANCES (LO-1) then finds the MIDPOINT meeting place (LO-3). Coordinates are read off a graph that does not travel with the stem.
Settles whether ABCD is a square using four sides and two diagonals - the stem itself says 'using distance formula'. Coordinates come from a figure that is not carried with the question.
XA:XY = 2:5 is converted to XA:AY = 2:3 and the section formula locates A before it is put into a line. Ratio conversion is the whole difficulty, so LO-2.
Ratio in which a general LINE divides a segment, found by substituting the k:1 point into the line. LO-2.
Ratio in which the y-axis divides a segment, from the abscissa of the dividing point being zero, plus the point itself. LO-2.
The parallelogram's unknowns come from the diagonals sharing a MIDPOINT (LO-3); the side lengths that follow are DISTANCES (LO-1). Both halves are asked.
Section formula at 3:1 with algebraic coordinates, solved for a and b. Given ratio, so LO-2.
The equilateral vertex A comes from equal SIDE LENGTHS (LO-1), and D is then placed so BACD is a rhombus, which is a diagonal-MIDPOINT argument (LO-3).
Isosceles proved from side lengths (LO-1) and the AREA then found from the vertices (C-4.2-LO-1). One of the very few items in this chapter that reaches C-4.2.
Equilateral triangle with its base on an axis: the apex follows from equating side lengths. The origin being the midpoint of QR is given rather than derived, so LO-1 carries the item.
Section formula at a given 1:2 ratio locates P, which is then substituted into a line to find k. Division in a given ratio, so LO-2.
A general k:1 point on PQ is written down and x + y = a + b falls out identically. Purely the section formula, in symbols.
Rhombus proved from four equal side lengths. Distance formula only; the diagonals' midpoints are not used, so LO-3 is out.
Derives the section formula and then applies it to find a ratio - the only item in the chapter that asks for the derivation itself. Squarely LO-2.
Classifies the triangle by comparing its three side lengths (LO-1), then measures a median, which needs the MIDPOINT of the opposite side first (LO-3).
